story_text.value:
It all started with a poster in our office that says "Fck it, ship it".

People really gravitate to the poster. Take pictures with it. Tell us, "we love the sentiment!"

So we decided: why not launch a shop?

Strive & Seek is a side project with our own designs for builders, hackers, founders, etc.

Some designs are more upbeat. Others lean into the more realistic challenges of building things: "Born to Code, Forced to Fundraise" is an example.

We shouldn't pretend building stuff that works, creates value and scales is easy. We hope Strive & Seek provides a bit of encouragement, when necessary, or simply does a good job of accurately describing the week you're having.

It all started with a simple "Fck it, ship it" poster. Now we'll see if anyone else enjoys the designs, messages and sentiment as much as we do.

Appreciate any feedback!

story_text.value:
I am the main developer of Ferry. The team I am part of began on the demoscene in the mid-90s, but for a long while we are mainly just an indie development studio.

Ferry started with me being forced to use macOS at my current workplace, which suddenly replaced a working environment I'd been using during professional career as a programmer: Windows for around 10 years, then Debian/KDE for the last 15 years.

Over that time, I'd grown very accustomed to Total Commander on Windows, and later Dolphin on Linux as a file manager, plus a collection of small but very useful tools I'd written for myself on Linux. Moving to macOS was quite an adjustment. I really struggled with Finder and the rather fragmented ecosystem of apps, especially when I couldn't find tools that covered the things I was used to having at my fingertips.

Having already written a few internal tools in Swift at work, I started to get familiar with the language while trying out several file managers for macOS without finding one that really suited all of my needs... So one thing led to another, and I eventually decided to build my own version of a better Finder (that's probably how most of the macOS file managers started their journey).

Obviously, the first versions were essentially a combination of a slightly improved dual-pane Finder spiced up with basic features from TC, but t'was more than good enough for me. Once I started sharing it with coworkers and friends they began suggesting features I hadn't even considered initially, many of which turned out to be genuinely useful.

I know there are quite a lot of file managers out there, so a "what makes Ferry different?" is a totally valid question.

Well, Ferry first and foremost tries to be as less opinionated and as much customizable as it's possible, so I have included A LOT of options for personalization. Eg. the layout, the UI, the menus, or the shortcuts are adjustable in many ways, you could even put together something which more or less resembles an old-school Norton Commander-style file manager with a modern toolset if that's your thing.

The app also includes a rather big collection of handy tools and tidbits which probably don't seem too interesting up until the point you run into a specific trivial task, and then you realize you have to search and install a tool for it.

Main features list: https://ferry.indus3.org/#ftrs

Another aspect that's important to me is how the app is made. Having been really involved in the demoscene, I wanted to handcraft as much code as possible and keep AI involvement to a minimum, while still using it to improve quality. Most of Ferry is still written manually, AI mainly helps with the boring parts: proofreading and translations, debugging, tests, temporary tools, code reviews and the site. LLMs have become so advanced that I'm honestly not sure whether this is a good or bad thing for software quality. My skills probably aren't quite on par with a modern LLM agent, but hopefully I can still build something useful and pragmatic by doing most of the work myself.

Licensing follows TC's approach: there's a reminder, but you can keep using the app for as long as you like (or until the reminder gets too annoying). Hopefully that's reasonable enough. But if I eventually become really happy with the codebase, I'll most likely release the source code too.

At this point, since there are plenty of features, I'm becoming much less interested in adding even more of them and rather focused on getting the existing ones as good as possible: size, stability, performance, memory consumption and above all, bugfixes and code quality. Of course I still listen to users, and if someone suggests a feature which is practical and it improves the UX, I try to include it into a future release.

Feel free to contact us, as suggestion and criticism is always welcome!

title.value: Show HN: Ferry, a highly customizable and feature-rich file manager for macOS

story_text.value:
Scribbles started as a guestbook and evolved into a drawing tool with a gallery for visitors' artwork. The idea is to create a place to draw a quick doodle without signing up and show off contributions, silly or serious. The canvas is in your web browser, and you can save your drawing as well as send it to me if you want to. I approve every submission before it goes in the gallery. Instead of having user accounts, visitors get a receipt code that allows them to remove their submission from the gallery later if they wish.

The project was built with Claude Code on my design over the course of a couple months. It originally started as a part of my personal site, but I expanded it to its own domain once I saw how much visitors engaged with the idea. The goal was to make a simple tool that makes drawing approachable, and one that can run well on any device.

I'll be in the thread to answer any questions or read feedback. Thanks for checking out my little site.

story_text.value:
Hi HN. MakeWorks 98 is a low stress game set in a simulation of a late 90s desktop.

You play by doing the job: answering mail in Lookout Express, chatting with simulated colleagues in Natter, adding up favours in the spreadsheet, and doing small Paint jobs. Over a year of in-game days you get promoted, people join and leave, and a daft office story goes on.

You can also slack off with Solitaire, FreeCell, Mahjong, Draughts, 2048, and a word puzzle. There are plenty of Easter eggs (try Run regedit). Some bits get unlocked by playing for a while or doing daft tasks.

Technical bits people might find interesting:

- Everything on screen is drawn by a GUI toolkit I written in C#. Windows, menus, tree views, list views, drag and drop and colour schemes all draw their own pixels, with bitmap fonts. Nothing uses native widgets or HTML. - The game uses raylib (Raylib CS wrapper) and via the browser as .NET WebAssembly (AOT) drawing to a canvas. - Saves live in IndexedDB as a zipped copy of the "C: drive". You can download that zip as a backup and restore it.

I made this after making the GUI toolkit, which I made because of my love of the aesthetic of this time.

I should mention that this doesn't work well on a phone sized screen; you really need a computer to play. I should also mention that I did use Claude Code to write a good chunk of this after I had established the drawing/widget core.

story_text.value:
Hi HN!

I recently saw HackerTube, which Andrej Karpathy posted here, and really liked it. Instead of YouTube’s algorithm, it uses videos recommended on HN as the pool. Using it, I liked that I only watched and got recommended actually worthwhile videos, not clickbait Shorts or sensational stuff that makes me curious about things I never cared about.

But it’s limited to videos that got posted on HN, so I built a new service called OOO.

Like HackerTube, videos play in an iframe. The difference is that users can upload their own collections, and when you subscribe to collections, only those become your video pool.

Oh, and you can also customize how recommendations are sorted. You can make multiple feeds too, each pulling from a different set of collections.

I had Opus make about 50 initial collections and watched through them myself. It was a pretty good experience.

So I’d love for you to try it and give me honest (even harsh) feedback. Feel free to upload your own collections too. All feedback is welcome.

story_text.value:
Hi HN. I made a lightweight app where you can add patient's cancer reports (pathology, scans, gene tests, even phone photos) and get a tactical plan based on care guidelines from US, Europe, India. The plan has precise, targeted drugs for their gene changes with FDA status, options beyond standard care, missing tests and matching trials. I've made sure (every) line traces to the reports or a primary source, and anything the reports don't say shows as missing.

Have kept it free for now.

It's pretty new, has gpt 5.6 luna as the backbone, has a bunch of evals written, so feedback and bug reports are very welcome.

PS: Pls email rohan@vivonco.com if you want to work together on precision oncology research.

Rohan (prev worked in cancer care in india, 7 years in the Bay Area in tech, Stanford)

story_text.value:
Hi all,

I started learning Piano a while ago, memorising songs from YouTube and graduating to learning classical pieces from sheet music that are too hard for me. It's typical, and you can express yourself through piece selection, and dynamics etc but this is quite limited. I reflected on why I want to play; to be able to sit and improvise, to freely express myself, to make my own music. So I created Noodle; she's a little companion you connect to your digital piano and she guides you through chord progressions, inversions, licks, and traditional scale exercises, guiding you to make nice sounding music.

Would appreciate any feedback, and I've included 20 redemption codes for the lifetime license at the end of the post.

Cheers, Rahil

story_text.value:
Hi HN. I'm Brian, I make Xmind, the most popular mind mapping app, since 2006. This is my new project Nico, a personal agent for the Mac.

Every huge companies are building personal agents right now. The part I think matters most is the two-agent structure, so that's what Nico is built around.

The front agent talks to you. Always available, only one session, one memory, continuously compaction, and it carries almost no tools, so it can answer fast.

The worker agent does the job. It picks up tasks the front agent puts in an inbox and reports back when they're done. It almost never talks to you; anything it needs goes through the front agent.

I think this is the real step forward, but the attention goes to the cloud computer. I get why: you can hand the agent a task from your phone. But, it also makes everything more complicated. People need to upload the entire environment while

So I built one with the cloud computer taken out. Nico is a native Mac app. You hold the right ⌘ key (or fn) and talk; the front agent answers by voice; the worker agent is pi (github.com/earendil-works/pi) runs by your own AI subscription, in a sandbox.

With computer-use (via cua-driver), browser-use (via a browser extension), and a built-in browser, she can clean up your desktop, or answer "why is my Mac so hot". If you say "this", she looks at the screenshot of the active window. Most tasks run without you; sending an email waits for your click.

The downside: when you're not at your Mac, you can't use it. I haven't figured out what to do about that.

Would you want a personal agent that only lives on your Mac?

title.value: Show HN: Nico – a two-agent type personal agent on your Mac

story_text.value:
Hi HN, we’ve created Mooring, an agentic development environment for Claude Code. We are really keen to get some thoughts and feedback from the community who are currently building with Claude Code.

An ADE is where you run AI coding agents and steer the work. It’s slightly different to a traditional IDE, where you write the code and AI may help. In an ADE, agents do the work, and you direct and review it.

It lets you build across multiple Claude sessions, several branches, speak notes, create task cards and gives great visibility for how fast your parallel sessions are using your limit, stopping cleanly at your plan limit.

At the moment it’s for Claude Code and macOS 26 on Apple silicon only. It’s free to use and we’re keen to show it to people and get feedback from people currently building with Claude Code.
